books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Proceedings of the IEEE, 2012 (radio stations and household ownership)

stimulus.text:
Radio in the United States, 1922–1930:

| Year | Licensed radio stations | Homes with a radio |
| 1922 | about 30 | fewer than 1 in 100 |
| 1923 | about 570 | 1 in 100 |
| 1930 | 618 | 40 in 100 |

Source: Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.7 (almost 600 licensed stations by 1923); Proceedings of the IEEE, 2012 (stations and household ownership); “Radio in the United States” (1 percent of homes in 1923).
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.7; Proceedings of the IEEE, 2012; and “Radio in the United States.”

stem: The table best shows that radio in the 1920s

options.text: reached most homes in its first year
options.misconception: In 1922 fewer than 1 home in 100 had a radio. Most homes came years later, not in the first year.

options.text: stayed a hobby of a few amateurs
options.misconception: By 1930, 40 homes in 100 had a radio, and stations numbered over 600. Radio had become a mass medium, not a hobby.

options.text: spread from a few stations to many homes
replaced newspapers as the main news source
options.misconception: The table says nothing about newspapers. Radio grew beside newspapers; it did not replace them in the 1920s.

rationales.A: In 1922 fewer than 1 home in 100 had a radio. Most homes came years later, not in the first year.
rationales.B: By 1930, 40 homes in 100 had a radio, and stations numbered over 600. Radio had become a mass medium, not a hobby.
rationales.C: Stations grew from about 30 to 618, and homes with radios from under 1 in 100 to 40 in 100. Radio spread from a few stations to many homes.
rationales.D: The table says nothing about newspapers. Radio grew beside newspapers; it did not replace them in the 1920s.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first row: about 30 stations, and fewer than 1 home in 100 with a radio.
2. Read the last row: 618 stations, and 40 homes in 100 with a radio.
3. Name the pattern: both columns grew fast, from almost nothing to a mass medium.
Remember: read a table row by row, and let the first and last rows set the size of the change.
